title: Merge k Sorted Lists
directAnswer: Two clean O(N log k) solutions (N = total nodes, k = number of lists). (1) Min-heap: push the head of every list into a priority queue keyed by value; repeatedly pop the smallest, append it to a dummy-headed result, and push that node's next. (2) Divide-and-conquer: pair up the k lists and merge each pair with the standard two-list merge, halving the count each round until one list remains. Both beat the naïve 'merge one at a time' O(N·k) by replacing the linear scan for the minimum with either a heap or balanced pairwise merging.

remember.pattern: Min-heap over list heads OR divide-and-conquer pairwise merge
remember.formula:
# Min-heap (O(N log k))
heap = [(node.val, i, node) for i, node in enumerate(lists) if node]
heapify(heap)
dummy = curr = ListNode(0)
while heap:
    val, i, node = heappop(heap)
    curr.next = node; curr = node
    if node.next:
        heappush(heap, (node.next.val, i, node.next))
return dummy.next
rules: Use a **dummy head** so appending the merged nodes never special-cases the first node.
Heap holds **at most k** entries (one live head per list), so each push/pop is `O(log k)` and total work is `O(N log k)`.
In Python, push a **tuple `(val, index, node)`** — the `index` tiebreaker stops `heapq` from trying to compare `ListNode` objects when values tie.
In Java, give `PriorityQueue` an explicit **comparator** `(a, b) -> a.val - b.val` (or `Integer.compare`) since `ListNode` isn't `Comparable`.
Divide-and-conquer merges in **pairs**, halving k each round → `log k` rounds, each touching all N nodes → `O(N log k)`.
**Skip null lists** when seeding the heap or the divide step — an empty input list contributes nothing and a null head must never be pushed/dereferenced.
Both approaches reuse the two-list **merge** primitive (Merge Two Sorted Lists) — know it cold.
whenToUse: Merge k already-sorted sequences (lists, streams, run files) into one sorted output
k-way merge step of external merge sort
Repeatedly needing the global minimum across k sorted sources → min-heap
Combining results from k shards/partitions that are each locally sorted
antiSignals: Only two lists → just use the single two-pointer merge, no heap needed
Lists are unsorted → sort first, or this k-way trick doesn't apply
Total size is tiny → concatenate-and-sort O(N log N) is simpler and competitive
You need O(1) extra space strictly → divide-and-conquer's recursion is O(log k) stack; heap is O(k)
remember.takeaway: Merge k Sorted Lists is the canonical k-way merge. The min-heap turns 'find the smallest of k heads' into an O(log k) operation; divide-and-conquer gets the same O(N log k) by merging in a balanced binary-tree shape. Both lean on the two-list merge — master that primitive and this hard problem becomes a composition exercise.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can beat the naïve O(N·k) by recognising this as a k-way merge — and whether you can implement either a heap keyed correctly (comparator / tuple tiebreaker) or a clean divide-and-conquer with the two-list merge as a subroutine.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Merging lists one-by-one into an accumulator (O(N·k)), pushing whole ListNodes into a Python heap (TypeError when values tie), or forgetting to skip null/empty input lists.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Name both O(N log k) solutions and compare their trade-offs (heap = O(k) space, streaming-friendly; divide-and-conquer = O(log k) stack, cache-friendly). Derive the complexity out loud and reuse the two-list merge as a named helper.

problemStatement:
You are given an array of `k` linked lists `lists`, where each list is sorted in ascending order.

*Merge all the lists into one sorted linked list and return its head.*

The result must itself be sorted in ascending order, and it should be built from the existing nodes (you may relink them).
constraints: Each lists[i] is sorted in ascending order
The sum of lists[i].length will not exceed 10⁴ (this is N)
understanding: We have k independent sorted lists and must produce one globally sorted list. The key realisation is that at every step the next node to emit is the smallest among the current heads of the k lists. The whole problem reduces to repeatedly finding that minimum head efficiently. Doing it by linear scan is O(k) per node → O(N·k); a heap makes it O(log k) per node → O(N log k); divide-and-conquer reaches the same bound by merging lists pairwise in a balanced tree. Some input lists may be empty (null heads) and must be ignored.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can any of the k lists be empty, or the whole array be empty?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — k can be 0, and individual lists can be null. I skip null heads when seeding the heap or recursing, and return null if there's nothing to merge.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I relink the existing nodes, or must I allocate new ones?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: I relink the existing nodes into the result — no new value nodes needed beyond a dummy head. That keeps space down to the heap (O(k)) or recursion stack (O(log k)).

clarifyingQuestions.question: Roughly how do k and N compare? Is k large?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: If k is large and N moderate, the heap's O(log k) per node matters. Both my solutions are O(N log k); I'd pick the heap for streaming sources and divide-and-conquer when recursion is fine and I want O(log k) extra space.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are duplicate values across lists allowed?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. The merge is stable enough for correctness; in Python I add an index tiebreaker so equal values never force a ListNode comparison.

examples.explanation: Three sorted lists merged: the two 1s come first, then 2, 3, the two 4s, 5, and 6.
No lists at all → empty result.
A single empty list → empty result. The lone null head is skipped.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: Both the min-heap and divide-and-conquer hit O(N log k). The one-at-a-time merge is the O(N·k) trap to avoid.

approaches.name: Min-Heap of List Heads (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: Lead with this when k may be large or sources stream in. Frame it as 'a priority queue always hands me the global minimum head in O(log k)'.
hints: At every step the next node to output is the smallest among the current heads of the k lists. What data structure gives you the minimum of k items and lets you replace it fast?
Seed a min-heap with the head of each non-empty list. Pop the smallest, append it to a dummy-headed result, and if that node has a next, push the next into the heap.

The heap never holds more than k nodes, so each pop/push is O(log k); across all N nodes that's O(N log k). In Python push (val, index, node) so equal values don't compare ListNodes; in Java pass a comparator.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each of the N nodes is pushed once and popped once. The heap size is bounded by k (one live head per list), so each operation costs O(log k). Total = N × O(log k) = O(N log k) time. The heap holds at most k entries → O(k) space (plus the O(1) dummy and pointers).
approaches.explanation:
The merge is driven by one repeated question: *of the current front nodes of all k lists, which is smallest?* A min-heap answers that in `O(log k)` and lets us swap in the next candidate just as cheaply.

**Why a heap and not a linear scan.** The naïve k-way merge scans all k heads to find the minimum each time it emits a node — `O(k)` per node, `O(N·k)` overall. A min-heap keeps the k candidate heads partially ordered so the minimum is always at the root (`O(1)` to read, `O(log k)` to remove). After we take the smallest node, the only new candidate is *that node's successor* in its own list, which we push in `O(log k)`. So we replace an `O(k)` scan with an `O(log k)` heap op — that single substitution is the whole optimisation.

**Why the heap size stays at k.** At any instant the heap contains at most one node per list: the current head of each list that still has nodes. We pop one and push at most one (its `next`), so the size never grows beyond `k`. That's why the log factor is `log k`, not `log N` — a meaningfully tighter bound when `k ≪ N`.

**Why the tiebreaker / comparator matters.** When two heads share a value, the heap must still order its entries. In Java, `ListNode` isn't `Comparable`, so we *must* supply a comparator `(a, b) -> Integer.compare(a.val, b.val)`. In Python, `heapq` compares tuples lexicographically; if we pushed `(val, node)` and two vals tied, it would fall through to comparing `ListNode` objects and throw `TypeError`. Pushing `(val, index, node)` with a unique `index` guarantees the comparison resolves on the integer index before it ever touches a node — a subtle but exam-critical detail.

**Why the dummy head.** As in every list-building problem, a sentinel removes the 'is this the first node?' branch. We append each popped node via `curr.next = node; curr = node` and return `dummy.next`. One more detail: the last node we append may still point into its old list, but because we always overwrite `curr.next` on the *next* append and the final node's old `next` was already consumed (or is null), the result is correctly terminated; defensively, you can set `curr.next = null` at the end.
approaches.insight: The heap converts 'minimum of k things, repeatedly, with cheap replacement' into a logarithmic operation — the defining use case for a priority queue. Recognising that the next output is always the minimum of the live heads is the entire leap; everything else is standard heap mechanics. The same shape appears in Smallest Range Covering Elements and Merge k sorted arrays/iterators.

dryRun.intro: Seed heap with the three heads keyed by value. Pop the min, append it, push its next. Heap holds ≤ 3 entries.

java.line: PriorityQueue<ListNode> pq = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> Integer.compare(a.val, b.val));
java.explanation: ListNode isn't Comparable, so we MUST supply a comparator ordering by node value.
Skip empty input lists — never push a null head into the heap.
Root of the heap is the global minimum among all current heads — O(log k) to remove.
Append the smallest node to the result and advance the build pointer.
The only new candidate is this node's successor in its own list — push it.
Defensively terminate the result so no stale link from the last node leaks through.
Skip the sentinel; return the real merged head.

python.explanation: Push (value, list-index, node); the index breaks ties so heapq never compares ListNode objects.
Skip null/empty lists when seeding the heap.
Pop the smallest entry; the value sorts first, the index resolves ties.
Append the popped node and move the build pointer onto it.
Push the successor from the SAME list (keep its original index i).
Return the node after the sentinel.

edgeCases.behavior: No heads pushed, heap empty, while loop skipped → return dummy.next = null.
The single head is null → skipped during seeding, heap stays empty → null result.
Push 1(L0) and 0(L2), skip the empty L1. Pop 0 then 1 → result [0, 1].

pitfalls: In Python, pushing (val, node) without an index — TypeError when two values tie and heapq compares ListNodes.
In Java, forgetting the comparator — ClassCastException because ListNode isn't Comparable.
Pushing null heads from empty lists — NullPointerException / wrong ordering.
Not terminating the final node's next, leaving a stale link into an old list.

approaches.name: Divide and Conquer — Pairwise Merge
approaches.whenToMention: Offer as the alternative O(N log k) with O(log k) stack and no heap. Frame it as 'merge sort's merge step, but the units are whole sorted lists'.
hints: You already know how to merge TWO sorted lists in O(total) time. How few times do you need to apply that to collapse k lists into one?
Pair the lists up: merge lists[0]+lists[1], lists[2]+lists[3], and so on. That halves the count each round. After log k rounds only one list remains.
Implement it recursively by splitting the array in half, merging each half, then merging the two results — exactly merge sort's structure with sorted lists as the elements.
approaches.complexityReasoning: There are log k merge rounds. In each round every one of the N nodes is touched exactly once across all the pairwise merges, so each round is O(N). log k rounds × O(N) = O(N log k) time. Recursion depth is log k → O(log k) stack space (the iterative pairwise variant is O(1) extra).
approaches.explanation:
Instead of a heap, we lean entirely on the two-list merge and apply it in a balanced binary-tree shape so that each node is merged through only `log k` levels.

**Why pairing beats one-at-a-time.** Merging lists sequentially into one accumulator re-walks the growing accumulator over and over: the first list's nodes get compared in every subsequent merge, giving `O(N·k)`. Pairwise merging fixes the imbalance. In round one we merge `k/2` independent pairs; in round two `k/4` pairs of the results; and so on. A given node participates in one merge per round, and there are only `log k` rounds — so each node is touched `log k` times total, yielding `O(N log k)`.

**Why it's literally merge sort on lists.** Classic merge sort splits an array in half, sorts each half, and merges. Here the 'elements' are already-sorted lists and the 'merge' is the two-sorted-list merge. We recurse on `lists[lo..mid]` and `lists[mid+1..hi]`, then merge the two returned lists. The recursion tree has depth `log k`, and the merge work summed across any level is `O(N)` — the same accounting that gives merge sort its `O(n log n)`.

**Why the two-list merge is the heart of it.** `mergeTwo(a, b)` walks both lists with a dummy head, always appending the smaller current node and advancing that list, then attaches whatever remains when one side empties. It runs in `O(len(a) + len(b))` and `O(1)` extra space. Getting this primitive exactly right — the dummy head, the `while a and b` loop, and the `curr.next = a or b` tail attach — is what makes the whole divide-and-conquer correct.

**Why the space profile differs from the heap.** There's no auxiliary heap, so the only extra memory is the recursion stack of depth `log k` → `O(log k)`. (An iterative version that repeatedly sweeps the array merging adjacent pairs uses `O(1)` extra.) That makes divide-and-conquer attractive when you want to avoid a heap's `O(k)` footprint, though both share the same time bound and reuse the same merge subroutine.
approaches.insight: Reframing 'merge k lists' as 'merge sort where the elements are sorted lists' instantly delivers the O(N log k) bound and reuses a primitive you already trust. Whenever you see 'combine k sorted things', think balanced pairwise merging or a heap — they're the two faces of k-way merging.

edgeCases.behavior: Guard returns null immediately — no recursion on an empty range.
Single list: lo == hi base case returns it unchanged with no merging.
mergeTwo treats null halves correctly — merging null with [1] just returns [1]; result [1].

pitfalls: Merging one list at a time into an accumulator — degrades to O(N·k).
Recursing on an empty range without the lists.length == 0 guard — index errors.
Using < instead of <= in mergeTwo loses stability (cosmetic here, but a habit worth keeping).
Forgetting to attach the leftover tail (curr.next = a or b) — drops the rest of one list.

commonMistakes: Merging the lists one at a time, yielding O(N·k) instead of O(N log k).
In Python, pushing whole ListNodes into the heap — TypeError when two values are equal.
In Java, omitting the PriorityQueue comparator — ListNode isn't Comparable.
Failing to skip null/empty input lists when seeding the heap or recursing.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Quadratic-ish one-at-a-time merge
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Folding lists into a single accumulator re-traverses the growing result on every merge, so early nodes are compared k times — O(N·k). Pairwise merging or a heap brings it to O(N log k).
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
result = None
for lst in lists:
    result = self._merge_two(result, lst)  # re-walks the accumulator each time
return result

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Pushing ListNodes into a Python heap
commonMistakesDetailed.why: heapq compares tuple elements left-to-right; if it reaches a ListNode (because two values tie) it raises TypeError since ListNode defines no ordering. A unique index between val and node resolves ties first.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: heapq.heappush(heap, (node.val, node))   # TypeError on equal vals
commonMistakesDetailed.good: heapq.heappush(heap, (node.val, i, node)) # index i breaks ties before node

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing comparator on a Java PriorityQueue
commonMistakesDetailed.why: PriorityQueue needs either Comparable elements or an explicit Comparator. ListNode is neither Comparable, so the default constructor throws ClassCastException at the first comparison.
commonMistakesDetailed.good: PriorityQueue<ListNode> pq = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> Integer.compare(a.val, b.val));

patternNote: Canonical k-way merge. The min-heap variant (O(k) space, streaming-friendly) and the divide-and-conquer variant (O(log k) stack, cache-friendly) both reach O(N log k) and both reduce to the two-list merge primitive. Recognise this shape in external merge sort, Smallest Range Covering Elements, and Kth Smallest in a Sorted Matrix.
